workload.description: 200k rps peak in one region: 90% CDN video-segment fetches across a two-tier edge, the rest watch-page/API, telemetry and a tiny upload CONTROL plane. The transcode farm is batch work and is deliberately outside this per-second model — see the transcode assumption.

components.name: CDN edge tier 1 — in-ISP caches (GGC): video segments + thumbnails
CDN edge tier 2 — Edge PoP / origin shield (absorbs tier-1 misses)

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 200,000 req/s peak in ONE region. 90% of requests are CDN video-segment fetches, 6% watch pages, 2% search/browse, 1% view beacons, ~1% engagement writes, 0.01% (20/s) video uploads.

assumptions.subject: cdn
assumptions.statement: Google's edge is TWO tiers and this file now models both: `cdn` is the in-ISP Google Global Cache layer and `edge_pop` is the Edge PoP / origin shield behind it, with the data-centre object store behind that (Google, 'Understanding Google Cloud network edge points'; the ISP-facing GGC docs). Only ONE of the two hit rates has anything published behind it: Google tells ISPs that GGC serves roughly 70-90% of their YouTube traffic, so the 15% tier-1 miss modelled here sits at the OPTIMISTIC end of that published range (85% offload), not at its midpoint. The midpoint of 70-90% offload is 80%, i.e. a 20% miss. This matters and is stated rather than smoothed over: at the true 20% midpoint the `edge_pop` tier's own N+1 redundancy claim fails — losing one of 3 units puts the survivors at 90%, over the 85% ceiling — and at the 30% miss the same source implies for a cold or long-tail catalogue, all 3 units run at 90% with none lost. The headline bottleneck (the Watch/API tier) is unaffected anywhere in that range. Read it as directional, not as a benchmark for your own CDN — it is offload measured AT GGC on Google's own fleet with more tiers behind it, not end-to-end origin offload. Google also states it does NOT pre-fill GGC: caches fill on demand, so a cold or long-tail catalogue misses more than this. The second number — that the Edge PoP absorbs 90% of those tier-1 misses, leaving 1.5% of segment requests to reach the origin — has NO published figure behind it at all and is the input the object store's load is most sensitive to. It replaces an earlier single-tier, wholly unsourced '96% hit rate' that put 7,200 rps on the origin and thereby made the object store a near-tie for this design's bottleneck on the strength of one uncited guess.

assumptions.subject: edge_pop
assumptions.statement: Three shield nodes at 20k rps each is a SIZING CHOICE, not a measurement: no per-PoP capacity figure is published, and a real Edge PoP is a facility rather than a box — read 'instances' here as independent shield capacity units. It is deliberately N+1: the tier still sits under the design ceiling for the tier-1 miss traffic when one unit is lost. Its 25 ms base latency (further away than an in-ISP cache, nearer than the origin) is likewise an assumption.

assumptions.subject: transcode
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED HERE, ON PURPOSE, AND NOT IN THE BILL BELOW. This file used to carry a transcode fleet inside the per-second request model at 0.5 tasks/s per worker x 320 workers. That is arithmetically self-consistent and physically impossible: it implies a whole 6-rendition encode costs ~12 CPU-seconds no matter how long the video is. Published encode rates: Google's Argos VCU paper (Ranganathan et al., ASPLOS '21) reports a 2-second 1080p VP9 chunk taking about 10 s to encode and needing 5-6 chunks in flight to keep up with real time — about 5 CPU-seconds per video-second per output — and the same paper states VP9 software is '6-8x slower and more expensive than H.264', so the cheapest published SOFTWARE case is roughly 0.7 CPU-seconds per video-second per output. Multi-output transcoding does not rescue it: that paper measures MOT throughput only 1.2-1.3x SOT, because sharing the decode does not share the encodes. At this file's 20 uploads/s, with an ASSUMED mean uploaded length of ~6 minutes (there is no published figure for that, and lower rungs of a ladder are cheaper than 1080p, so treating all six at the 1080p rate overstates), a six-rung ladder is of the order of 30,000 CPU cores held continuously at the H.264 floor and several times that at the VP9 rate — tens of times the fleet this file used to declare. That gap is why Google built a hardware transcoder instead of buying cores. The correct way to size an encode farm is against a backlog-drain DEADLINE, not a per-second arrival rate; sibling blueprint video_streaming.json states the same rule and excludes it the same way. What remains in the model is job submission: 6 rendition jobs per upload on the queue row (visit_prob 6.0). (Labelled ASSUMPTION rather than GAP only because this library reserves the GAP label for the byte-volume disclosures the gate computes; read it as a declared gap.)

assumptions.subject: upload
assumptions.statement: Raw bytes go client -> object store DIRECTLY via a presigned URL; the upload service only issues the URL and commits metadata (this is how YouTube's own resumable upload protocol works). The engine therefore models the upload CONTROL PLANE, not the byte transfer — which is why that tier is almost idle: it handles roughly one request per upload, not the gigabytes.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The cost line is COMPUTE ONLY. CDN egress, object-storage GB and per-request fees are deliberately left at zero: at this volume nobody pays $0.09/GB list egress, so multiplying list rates by petabytes would produce a confidently wrong bill.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: THE TOTAL BELOW IS SERVING COMPUTE ONLY, AND IT IS A FLOOR, NOT WHAT A VIDEO PLATFORM COSTS. The transcode farm — of the order of 10^4 CPU cores at this upload rate (see the transcode assumption), and in reality the largest compute line any video platform has — is not modelled and so is not priced. CDN egress and object-storage bytes are zero by the note above. Removing the old, fabricated 320-worker transcode row removed most of this file's former compute bill; that is a correction to a wrong number, not a saving, and nobody should read the drop as one. (Labelled ASSUMPTION rather than GAP only because this library reserves the GAP label for the byte-volume disclosures the gate computes; read it as a declared gap.)

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Redis runs as a 2-node HA pair, sized for failover rather than throughput — hence its low utilisation. That is a deliberate reference-design choice, not headroom you should bank on.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Single PostgreSQL primary at ~8k rps for engagement writes and upload metadata; reads are served by 2 replicas behind the Redis cache.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: HISTORICAL CORRECTION for anyone copying this shape: YouTube's metadata was never PostgreSQL. It ran MySQL, sharded from 2010 behind the Vitess routing proxy — which was built AT YouTube precisely because the read replicas, and then the primary, ran out of capacity (vitess.io project history). The single primary modelled here is a teaching simplification and it is the exact failure mode Vitess exists to fix. The engine already flags it as a single point of failure; at anything approaching this write rate you shard, and this row stops being one box.

assumptions.subject: latency
assumptions.statement: The upload flow now measures the CONTROL PLANE only — issue a resumable-upload URL, commit metadata, enqueue six rendition jobs — which is why it is renamed upload_control_plane. It is NOT time-to-publish, and no figure on it should be read as how long a video takes to appear: Google tells uploaders that processing runs from minutes to hours depending on length and resolution, and the encode arithmetic in the transcode note is why. An earlier version of this file reported a tens-of-seconds 'time-to-publish' on this flow. That number was an artefact of pricing batch encode work as a per-second request queue — the engine's exponential-tail model is calibrated for request queues, not batch pipelines — and it has been removed rather than re-stated.

assumptions.subject: bottleneck
assumptions.statement: SENSITIVITY — read this before you go and optimise whatever the engine names. Which component binds here is a judgement about UNCITED INPUTS, not a measurement. As this file stood before this revision, three rows (the Watch/API tier, the object store and the transcode fleet) sat within about four percentage points of one another, so any one of the three unsourced numbers behind them flipped which component a reader would go and fix. Two of those three have now been re-derived — transcode has left the request model, and the origin now sits behind a second edge tier — which separates the field; the engine reports the current margin and any contenders itself, so trust that output and not this sentence. What has NOT changed is that the Watch/API tier's 2,000 rps per node is an ASSUMPTION with no load test behind it, and that the unmodelled ranking service (below) sits squarely on that same path. Re-derive per-node capacity from your own measurements before treating any named bottleneck as settled.

assumptions.subject: recommender
assumptions.statement: NOT MODELLED, and plausibly the largest real cost of a watch page. YouTube's home and watch surfaces are driven by a two-stage candidate-generation + ranking deep neural network (Covington, Adams & Sargin, RecSys 2016 — a decade old now, so treat it as directional about the SHAPE, not the cost). This design serves watch_page from Redis plus a SQL read replica, which is the metadata lookup, not the recommendation. There is no published per-request compute figure for that ranker, so nothing here is sized for it and no number below includes it; the honest statement is that it is missing and probably material, which matters precisely because it sits on the path of the tier this design leans on hardest. Budget for it separately. (Labelled ASSUMPTION rather than GAP only because this library reserves the GAP label for the byte-volume disclosures the gate computes; read it as a declared gap.)

_library.summary: Video platform: presigned-URL upload, a six-rendition transcode fan-out submitted to a job bus (the encode farm itself is batch and out of the request model), and two-tier CDN segment delivery in front of a cached metadata tier.
